By Abigail Mihaly Great Lakes researchers warn that changing Lake Ontario’s name is a costly waste of time that complicates longstanding collaboration to manage and protect an iconic water body named by indigenous people before either the United States or Canada were founded. The August 27 executive order signed by President Trump directs the federal government to change Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America across its maps, documents, and communications. The order comes amid trade disputes with the U.S.’ northern neighbor, which Trump slammed for “ripping us off.” Trump’s order says the new name, Lake America, intends to recognize the lake as a key American economic resource that has shaped the nation’s history. Tribal leaders, though, say Trump’s effort to change the name erases their ties to the region after a history of removal from the area. Federal Water Tap Weekly digest spotting trends in U.S. government water policy. Delivered every Monday. Sign up The name Ontario predates both Canada and the United States. It comes from Iroquoian words meaning “big”, “beautiful,” “shining” or “sparkling” lake, depending on the translation. While the exact origin of the name is disputed, many experts say Ontario comes from a Wendat word Ontari’io, while others say it comes from languages spoken by the Haudenosaunee or Mohawk indigenous groups that also spoke languages in the Iroquoian family. It’s not the first time Trump has renamed a body of water. Last year, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico to be renamed to the Gulf of America. One poll conducted by Marquette University Law School showed 71 percent of Americans disapproved of the renaming. Trump’s order renaming the Gulf of Mexico also raised questions about who would have to follow it. In one especially fraught example, Trump attempted to curtail the Associated Press’ access to the White House because the outlet continued to use the term “Gulf of Mexico” after his order changing its name.
